did_you_know.text: The speaker uses three images of protection: the Lord is his “rock of refuge,” “rock,” and “fortress”—a stable and secure place of refuge.
Trust in the Lord is presented as an enduring hope: the speaker says that the Lord has been his confidence since his youth, not only in a particular time of trouble.

The speaker describes his relationship with the Lord as one that has accompanied him from the beginning of his life—“from birth” and “from my mother’s womb”—and therefore the Lord’s praise is always on his lips.

The speaker says, “I have become a sign to many.” The chapter does not explain whether this refers to deliverance, suffering, or faith, but it is clear that his life has become a testimony visible to many.
The request not to be abandoned “in the time of old age” adds a dimension of facing physical weakness and the loss of strength.
Even after describing the threat from his enemies, the speaker declares, “But I will always hope.” Hope in the Lord is presented as perseverance, not merely a momentary response.

The Lord is described as the speaker’s teacher since his youth: “God, you have taught me from my youth.” This teaching is also connected with telling the next generation about the Lord’s wonderful deeds.

The speaker asks to continue proclaiming the Lord’s power even in old age, so that he can tell the coming generation about it. In this way, the chapter emphasizes the passing on of faith and memory from one generation to the next.
The expression “from the depths of the earth” portrays trouble as a descent into the deep. In contrast, the speaker asks the Lord to revive him and raise him up again.
Praise in the chapter is expressed through actual music: the speaker mentions playing the harp and the lyre, rather than relying on words alone.
